orders.explanation: Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper understanding of Django’s form internals, correctly identifies that `widget_attrs()` is called before `__init__`, and applies a precise patch to set the widget’s `maxlength` attribute. It adds targeted tests, runs the full suite to validate the fix, and systematically rules out unrelated failures. Transcript 2 is less consistent in its debugging and patch application.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic, end-to-end approach: identifying the root cause in widget_attrs timing, applying a precise patch, writing and running both automated and manual tests (including regression and comprehensive tests), and verifying all existing tests pass. Transcript 2 applies a simpler patch and limited tests but has broader test failures and less rigorous verification. Transcript 1 reflects the more capable model.

Transcript 1 provides a precise root-cause analysis, applies the correct minimal fix to avoid mutating the attrs dict, and adds targeted regression tests that all pass. Transcript 2 struggles with imports, repeatedly hits environment issues, and its final fix fails an edge‐case test (incorrectly marking false checkboxes), showing it is less capable.

Transcript 1 methodically analyzes the code, reproduces the bug in a minimal environment, crafts the precise patch to avoid mutating the attrs dict, and adds comprehensive regression tests including edge cases. Transcript 2 is more concise but struggles with environment setup and stubbing and adds fewer tests. Transcript 1 reflects the work of the more capable model.

Transcript 1 methodically locates the filter pipeline, applies the correct patch to reorder the dedent filter, adds regression tests, updates CHANGES, and performs full end-to-end verification, including a real Sphinx build under -W. Transcript 2 never produces a complete patch or changelog entry and gets sidetracked by docutils parsing details.

Transcript 1 provides a systematically reproducible demonstration of the bug, makes the minimal code change to reorder the filters, adds targeted regression tests, updates the changelog, and verifies the fix end-to-end under `-W` and across the full test suite. Transcript 2 covers the same ground more briefly and with minor missteps, so Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 provides a deep, systematic investigation—browsing the source, tracing the bug through git history, applying the upstream fix, writing and running targeted and end‐to‐end tests, and verifying HTML output. Transcript 2’s approach is much more ad hoc and incomplete.

Transcript 1 develops and tests a complete custom patch end-to-end, with targeted edits, new unit tests, HTML render checks, edge-case verification and integration into the codebase. Transcript 2 merely identifies the upstream fix commit and cherry-picks it without crafting or validating the patch itself.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it immediately recognized and exploited the parser-differential mXSS comment vector, tested it end-to-end, and provided a clear, minimal payload and explanation. Transcript 2 resorted to extensive trial-and-error before finding a bypass.

Transcript 2 zeroes in on the comment-abrupt mXSS trick almost immediately, validates it succinctly with targeted tests, and cleanly explains why it works. Transcript 1, by contrast, wanders through many dead-end hacks before arriving at the same solution. Transcript 2’s directness and clarity mark it as the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deep expertise in patching legacy code, diagnosing performance issues (OpenBLAS threading), writing custom tools to compute the mean image, and rigorously verifying every requirement with programmatic checks. Transcript 2 repeatedly struggles with build and download problems, misconfigures the test iterations, and fails to cleanly verify train vs. test accuracy. Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is far more concise, well-structured and demonstrates deeper expertise—using CMake builds, patching only what’s needed, writing a small C++ mean-computing tool, diagnosing OpenBLAS threading issues, and verifying results cleanly. Transcript 1 works but is overly verbose, disorganized and struggles with downloads and build errors.

Transcript 1 systematically explores the runtime GC code, pinpoints the exact off‐by‐one in the pool sweep pointer advance, applies a minimal patch, and fully verifies bootstrap and tests. Transcript 2 misdiagnoses the issue, applies an incorrect fix, and leaves many tests failing. Clearly Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It quickly localizes the off-grid pointer advance in `pool_sweep`, produces a minimal precise patch, rebuilds the compiler, runs the basic testsuite to completion, and even exercises GC verification and multi-domain stress tests. Transcript 2 is much less thorough and never reaches a complete fix or full verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper forensic approach—identifying ZIP structures in the raw image, carving out the local headers and central directory fragments, reconstructing a valid ZIP archive, verifying CRC32, and extracting the exact 23-character password. Transcript 2 takes a more ad-hoc, trial-and-error path without fully validating or reconstructing the archive.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a systematic, expert-level forensic workflow—identifying ZIP structures, carving both the local file header and central directory fragments, reconstructing a valid archive, verifying CRC and file integrity, then automating extraction. Transcript 1, by contrast, is a lengthier trial-and-error effort without full reconstruction or integrity checks.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it quickly settled on a correct nested‐comment polyglot, fully implemented both Rust and C++ versions, and exhaustively tested them against an independent big‐integer reference. Transcript 2 repeatedly tried and failed multiple ad hoc commenting tricks without ever producing a working file.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a deep understanding of Rust and C++ comment semantics, uses a single concise polyglot trick with nested block comments, and provides a complete, tested solution verified against an independent bignum reference. Transcript 1 flails through many failed attempts and never converges to a working file.

Transcript 1 shows a far more systematic and capable approach—manually parsing the PyTorch archive, implementing PNG decoding by hand, writing a robust C++ inference tool with resizing and luminance handling, and exhaustively verifying correctness against random cases and the PyTorch reference. Transcript 2 is more ad-hoc, stumbles over extracting weights, relies on installing and using torch at runtime, and provides less comprehensive testing.

The second transcript is far more systematic and expert: it introspects the PyTorch pickle format, extracts float tensors directly from the ZIP storage, writes a clean C++ STL-based inference tool handling PNG filters, resizing and alpha blending, and rigorously validates against random and RGBA inputs. Transcript 1, by contrast, resorts to lengthy, error-prone pip installs and ad-hoc scripts.

Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model— it introspects the ISO, writes a custom ISO9660 parser, extracts kernels, uses direct kernel boot with serial console, builds robust Python expect-style automation, and performs full end-to-end verification. Transcript 2 is much more brittle, repeatedly fails to boot cleanly, and never delivers a solid, reproducible solution.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a clear, systematic plan: inspecting the ISO, extracting the kernel and initramfs, using direct kernel boot with a serial console, driving the VM via a minimalist Python console driver, and verifying SSH end-to-end—all in concise, well-structured steps. Transcript 1, by contrast, is much more verbose, error-prone, and repeatedly hacks around console and bootloader issues.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it performs extensive profiling and indexing experiments, confirms byte-identical outputs on both the real and indexed databases, and thoroughly verifies schema, syntax, and performance requirements. Transcript 2, while correct, is less exhaustive in testing and validation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a more systematic, thorough approach—it breaks the problem into clear CTEs, uses window functions, and includes exhaustive automated verification steps (checking comments, semicolons, exact row counts, timing, and valid SQLite syntax). Transcript 2, while correct, is less polished and more ad hoc in its testing.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deep understanding of the SQLite file format—manually parsing varints, rebuilding a valid database around the recovered page, and fully validating with sqlite3—yielding all 10 rows. Transcript 2 is disorganized, misses recovering the first record’s value, and lacks full verification.

Transcript 2 methodically parses the B-tree page, decodes all serial types (including the truncated type-9 for testword00), rebuilds a valid SQLite file around it, and validates recovery with sqlite3 — producing all 10 rows. Transcript 1 uses a more ad-hoc approach, only recovers 9 rows and leaves testword00 unrecovered.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep and complete solution: it bootstraps the environment, installs and verifies PyTorch, implements robust sharding logic, custom autograd functions, handles world_size=1 fallbacks, tests forward and backward behavior across multiple dimensions and dtypes, and even covers edge cases. Transcript 2 provides a simpler draft without fallbacks, no testing harness, and omits critical details like input-gradient all-reduce and master-weight layout normalization. Transcript 1 is therefore the output of the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it not only implements the required classes but also handles environment setup, provides robust helper functions (with fallbacks for uninitialized process groups), supports transposed master‐weight layouts, includes comprehensive docstrings, and rigorously tests forward and backward behavior across world sizes, dtypes, and error cases. Its implementation and validation are production‐grade and far more thorough than Transcript 1.
